articles.title: Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed
articles.author: Allissa V. Richardson, Associate Professor of Journalism, USC Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism
paras: There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.
The auction blocks. The cotton fields. The lynching trees. The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.
And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected Georgia’s first Black woman governor. The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.
Bottoms has traced her ancestry back five generations to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia.
An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.
The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?

Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy.
The children who deserved a future
I keep thinking about the little children.

Between 1979 and 1981, Atlanta was terrorized by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.

The murders unfolded just years after Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated, although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.
That distinction matters. So does the fear.

Bottoms was born in 1970. She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.
What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.
Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future.

Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer.
And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.
The woman who sowed the seeds
This victory belongs, in no small measure, to democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams. Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers.

Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She lost both races. But through the New Georgia Project and Fair Fight, organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation, and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.

And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row headed by a Black Democratic woman. There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself.

Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.
And as a scholar of Black media history, I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: Charlotta Bass.
In 1952, Bass became the first Black woman nominated for vice president of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket.
The future Charlotta dared to imagine
Before the Voting Rights Act in 1965, before the March on Washington in 1963, before Jackson was elected mayor in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass.

A Black newspaper publisher who confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence in her four-decade ownership of The California Eagle, Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.

Bass ran when a Black woman entering the White House seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.
What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here?

History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state she promised to bring about.

For generations, Black women have been asked to save a democracy that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.
And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia.

The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.
And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.

articles.title: Labour’s immigration dilemma: with social care exceptions, the party is trying to have it both ways
articles.author: Erica Consterdine, Senior Lecturer in Public Policy, Lancaster University
paras: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s headline announcement on immigration centred on how long someone must spend in the UK before they can be granted indefinite leave to remain (ILR). She said this period will double from five to ten years – but social care workers will be exempt. This proposal was widely expected, but exempting social care workers is a U-turn for the government.

The proposals were met with a mixed response. Some on the left said the qualifying period is too high, while others on the right claimed the plans were too lax on immigration by exempting care workers.

Many migrants came to the UK on the understanding that five years of lawful residence would provide a path to settlement. So the government’s decision to retrospectively change those terms raises serious questions about fairness, trust and the legitimacy of immigration policy.

The UK is now moving towards one of the toughest settlement and naturalisation systems in Europe. In fact, this direction is more readily associated with the political right than a Labour government that presents itself as committed to equality, workers’ rights and social justice. So where are we now with immigration policy, and what does this shift tell us about British politics?

The tough naturalisation requirements come off the back of 16 years of restrictive rhetoric on immigration across the political spectrum. From 2010, the Conservative-led coalition government set a pledge to reduce net migration from hundreds of thousands to the tens of thousands. And since then, successive administrations and opposition parties have attempted to outflank each other on tough immigration talk.

The last Conservative government lurched towards nativist, exclusionary rhetoric, and draconian policy proposals in a bid to outmanoeuvre Reform UK. The result has been to keep immigration high on the public agenda (though with ebbs and flows following Brexit and COVID).

Yet despite the tough talk, the combination of an economy that needs migrant labour as well as humanitarian schemes for citizens of Hong Kong and Ukraine, took net migration to the highest level on record. This was in 2023, the year before the Conservatives left office.

Critically, while previous governments talked tough on immigration, Brexit left major shortages in the labour market, especially in some of the low-paid jobs that many Britons do not want to do. As a result, a number of policy schemes were introduced to plug these gaps, including the health and care visa.

This scheme proved popular, resulting in 106,000 visas being issued to social care workers (the figure excludes their dependants) in 2023. But since then, more scrutiny on sponsors and the decision to stop dependants coming to the UK on this visa have led to sharp declines.

Labour has long been dogged on immigration. The party spent most of its years in opposition apologising for apparent mistakes made in office over the managed migration programme. This was a series of policies that resulted in one of the most expansive immigration policies in Europe.

And ideologically, immigration has always been a headache for Labour. Like other social democratic parties, Labour is torn between its protectionist trade union roots, which favour tighter borders, and its rights-based tradition of protecting migrants.

The dilemma is further complicated by Labour’s neoliberal turn since the Blair era, which saw globalisation as inevitable and embraced flexible labour migration as a way of controlling inflation. In short, Labour has been complicit in deepening a labour market that depends on on migration for its workforce, while using the “secure borders” rhetoric.

These ideological tensions are reflected in the make-up of both the Labour party and its electorate, bringing together members and constituents with competing values and priorities – the “beer drinkers” and the “wine drinkers”. And they are precisely why the new rules contain a mixed bag of restrictions and concessions on social-care visas.

Andy Burnham’s government has faced this tension head on, with many in the party lambasting Mahmood’s pursuit of high thresholds for naturalisation. Prominent figures including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had accused Mahmood of “pulling the rug” from underneath people. This intra-party tension resulted in the decision to exempt social care workers.

Policies that increase immigration are never generally vote winners. But social democratic parties have a choice whether to keep quiet on the issue, accommodate pressures from the right, or attempt to walk a middle ground of selective immigration.

Former prime minister Keir Starmer was accused of echoing right-wing rhetoric and produced the restrictive white paper from which the new policies stem. In practice, Labour’s approach is built on contribution-based residency – the more you earn the longer you can stay.

So far, Burnham has largely sailed the same ship, maintaining Mahommod as home secretary and changing little of the direction on immigration. Yet his recent comments on humanitarian schemes and reopening the debate on free movement suggest that the tide might be beginning to turn. Mahmood’s U-turn on social care workers might be part of this shift.

articles.title: What Tommy Robinson’s conviction tells us about the cost to journalists reporting in the public interest
articles.author: Tom Felle, Associate Professor of Journalism, University of Galway
paras: During the unrest that followed the 2024 Southport murders, British tabloid the Daily Mail reported on the activities of far-right activist Tommy Robinson. The story was covered by freelance reporter Andrew Young, and edited by the Mail’s own Jacob Dirnhuber.

On October 28, Robinson was convicted for threatening and harassing Young and Dirnhuber. A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London found Robinson guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence, an offence with a maximum sentence of ten years. The judge will sentence him on December 16.

Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, hired private investigators to find the journalists’ home addresses. He messaged Dirnhuber saying “I’ll be knocking at your door”, and told Young by phone “I’m coming to get you”. He also posted images of Dirnhuber outside his home, and of Young’s family.
Before Robinson’s conviction, Young was given a close protection officer, while Dirnhuber was forced to move house.

Anyone is entitled to criticise the Daily Mail or challenge its reporting. In a democratic society, any member of the public must be free to challenge what journalists publish. But journalists must also be free to report without fearing threats of violence, whether online or in their homes.

In reality, threats to reporters’ homes and families, along with online abuse and physical intimidation, have become so pervasive that they are treated as part of the job in Britain and well beyond it.

Few of these cases end up in front of a jury, yet Robinson’s conviction shows that the law can respond. Prosecutors told an earlier hearing that none of the alleged harassment contained a direct threat of violence, and the jury still convicted.

Robinson’s victims had a national newspaper behind them, but many journalists have no such support. When threats make journalists or their editors think twice about a story, the public loses out, usually without ever knowing.

The Robinson case is one among many, and around the world journalists are increasingly under threat for doing their jobs. The Committee to Protect Journalists found a record 129 journalists and media workers were killed in 2025, more than three-quarters of them in conflict settings.
Europe is not immune: hired killers murdered Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta in 2017, and Ján Kuciak in Slovakia in 2018, both investigative journalists.

Most threats never come near that point, but they are very common. In a 2020 global survey by UNESCO and the International Center for Journalists, 73% of the women journalists who responded had experienced online attacks, and one in five reported being attacked or abused offline in connection with it.

In research commissioned by the UK government and published in July this year, 72% of the 531 journalists surveyed had experienced harassment, abuse, threats or legal intimidation. Among those affected, almost half said safety concerns had made them hesitate before reporting certain stories.
These figures should concern anyone who relies on journalists to uncover what those in power would prefer to keep quiet.

Online abuse is far more pervasive than physical violence, and it takes a heavy toll. Among those affected in the aforementioned UK government survey, 78% had faced online abuse, compared with 11% who had been physically attacked. Just over half said safety concerns had damaged their wellbeing, and almost one in four had considered leaving journalism.

Female journalists are at an increased risk of being targeted. In a 2026 UN Women study, nearly a quarter of female journalists and media workers surveyed had been diagnosed with or treated for anxiety or depression linked to online violence. Some 45% said they self-censored on social media to avoid abuse – a 50% increase on 2020 – and more than one in five self-censored in their day-to-day work.
My own research on abuse of women in Irish politics raises a related question about who can afford to stay visible in public life when doing so exposes them to threats.

Reporting the abuse often brings little relief. Only 17% of affected journalists in the UK government survey had gone to the police, and a little over one in four of those found it effective. Of those who reported to online platforms, just 5% found that route effective.

The Daily Mail deserves credit for standing by its journalists, but not every news organisation can afford to do the same, and many freelancers have no one to call. If reporters fear for their safety because of online or offline threats, stories will go untold, and those in power will face fewer questions. Democracy will suffer as a result, and we all lose out.

articles.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting bloc than some other Democratic candidates
articles.author: Christine Slaughter, Assistant Professor of Political Science, Boston University
paras: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals, as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black.

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide.

About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results. Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms, up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.
In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes, which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County.
Statewide support is holding steady
In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3%, from 50.6% in 2020, as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024.

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll.

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed. NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson, who won the governorship over Republican John James.
Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement.
Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate.

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity. Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates.

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination. If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.
My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations.

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program, while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience. El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries.

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election. Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day.
“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.

articles.title: How Amendment 3, vaccine mandates and school vouchers will shape Florida under the leadership of Byron Donalds
articles.author: Liv Coleman, Professor of Political Science and International Studies, University of Tampa
paras: In the midst of what pundits are calling a blue tsunami nationwide, Florida remained resolutely red, electing Republican Byron Donalds as its first Black governor and sending Republican Ashley Moody back to the U.S. Senate.
Donalds ran on a promise to continue the legacy of his predecessor, Gov. Ron DeSantis.

His victory was not as easily won as polls had predicted. In the week leading up to the election, polls put him at 4 points over his opponent, Democrat David Jolly. In the end, Donalds won by 1.3 points – about 107,000 votes.

I’m a political scientist who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. We can see based on Donalds’ campaign promises the direction in which he plans to lead the state.
Amendment 3 shakes things up
Donalds’ term as governor will start with a major change: On Nov. 3, Floridians voted to pass Amendment 3 to the state constitution.
This will cause a shift in the state’s long-standing commitment to home rule, the principle that local governments, such as cities and counties, should be able to set policy on local issues.

The amendment limits local government spending from tax revenue to core categories such as public safety, schools and natural resources. With a lower tax base, some local governments in rural areas may not be able to maintain basic services and might need help from the state.
DeSantis has called for a special session to address Amendment 3 before Donalds takes office.
DeSantis has said he plans to restrict home rule by stopping local governments from trying to raise revenue through additional taxation at the local level.
Donalds supported the amendment, and it will give him and the Legislature the opportunity to redistribute tax funding throughout the state.

This election has changed the makeup of the state Legislature, though, with the GOP losing its supermajority in the Florida House of Representatives, which requires holding 80 out of the 120 seats. This change in the Legislature could make it more difficult for Donalds to control the agenda in Tallahassee the way DeSantis did during his second term, when he had a supermajority in both houses of the Legislature.

Donalds has affirmed that he supports the big steps DeSantis has taken to limit home rule – such as limiting local control over land development and removing local elected officials from office – and plans to take executive authority further, scheduling more DOGE audits of local government and removing more elected officials as he sees fit.
When it comes to data centers, on the other hand, Donalds has said he favors local communities deciding whether to allow them to be built nearby.
Florida health policy on vaccine mandates

One of the first choices awaiting Donalds will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position created in 2007. The position comes with the power to declare public health emergencies, forcibly quarantine people and set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of seven childhood vaccine mandates.

As part of his conservative remake of Florida policies, DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, Dr. Joseph Ladapo, to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading medical freedom advocate and vaccine skeptic.

Ladapo opposes all vaccine mandates. He also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to drop mandates for four vaccines required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, the state allows exemptions only for approved religious or medical reasons.
The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics opposes the rule change on public health grounds.

Donalds has long opposed vaccine mandates and says that he did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine. He supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change to reduce school vaccination mandates and said during his campaign that he is open to reappointing Ladapo as surgeon general.

The Florida Legislature, however, will limit how far Donalds can push vaccine policy. The Legislature has mandated measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law.

One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of universal vouchers by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows parents of any income level to use US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence, for their children’s private or homeschooling education.

The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an estimated $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2026. State auditors have identified accountability problems in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced declining enrollment, with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.

Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program. He has expressed an interest in making Florida “the model state for school choice” by allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace.

His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a network of for-profit charter schools and advocates nationally for school choice. Whether the Donaldses will divest from the charter school business during the governor-elect’s term remains to be seen.

Already, the governor-elect has indicated that he might work with the Legislature to change the way the Florida Education Finance Program funds K-12 schools, allowing districts to spend funds with more flexibility.

During his campaign he also proposed a universal scorecard for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.

Donalds can also influence state education policy by appointing the seven members of the Board of Education and then recommending a candidate for commissioner of education for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the Florida Department of Education and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.
They board could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, as the DeSantis administration has done in the past.
During his campaign, Donalds attempted to distance himself from President Donald Trump, whose policies have proven unpopular even in red states such as Florida.

But in his victory speech on the evening of Nov. 3, Donalds proudly announced that he had received a congratulatory call from the president. “Mr. President,” he said to a cheering crowd, “I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red.”
This story is an update of a story published on Oct. 28, 2026. Read more of our stories about Florida.
Liv Coleman is affiliated with the Manatee County Democratic Party.

articles.title: Domestic abusers don’t always stop in the home – partners’ friends and family can become victims too
articles.author: Morag Kennedy, Senior Lecturer in Criminology and Criminal Justice, Nottingham Trent University
paras: Intimate partner abuse occurs between two distinct parties: the victim and the perpetrator. But the harm done can be much more complicated than this. It often spills over to affect families, friends and many others in the victim’s life.

Within the traditional criminal justice system in the UK and beyond, this concept of two distinct parties is referred to as the “victim-perpetrator dichotomy”. The majority of research on intimate partner abuse focuses on the primary victims of harm – the person who is suffering at the hands of their partner or spouse. Many of these primary victims will seek support from family and friends.

These “informal supporters” can also include colleagues and neighbours. And given that intimate partner abuse affects one in four women in England and Wales (one in six men), it is reasonable to assume that millions of people are supporting relatives, friends or acquaintances through these experiences.

Despite this, research on the “co-victims” of intimate partner abuse is limited, and this is even scarcer in cases that involve homicide. My research examines co-victims of intimate partner homicide – the people who have been bereaved by the killing. For every person who is killed by their intimate partner, around six to ten family members are likely to be affected by the death.

Needless to say, losing a loved one to a violent unexplained death is incredibly difficult to process. The tragic events can also come with major life changes, such as unexpected childcaring responsibilities when the victim was a parent.
What affected families say

My research focused on intimate partner homicide in England and Wales. Bereaved families have shared their stories of how the harms of the perpetrator can “overspill” and create further victims. This can be understood through the lens of coercive control, a well-established framework for understanding, identifying, evidencing and prosecuting both intimate partner abuse and homicide.

It is made up of four elements – the possibility of physical violence, intimidation, isolation and control. I found that intimidation tactics can spill over into families of victims long before the primary victim is killed by the perpetrator.

These family members experience coercive control often at the same time as their loved one suffers it, and as such become victims of the same perpetrator. This can result in similar harms as the primary victim experiences, but may have a different outcome. In their case it could, for example, manifest in family tension rather than a physical attack.
How co-victimisation works
As an academic who specialises in violence against women and girls, I interviewed eight families bereaved by intimate partner homicide to find out how intimidation tactics worked.

Shena* whose daughter and first grandchild were killed in 2013, spoke of being victimised while supporting her daughter through an abusive relationship. She experienced death threats, threats of rape and was stalked by the perpetrator while he was also abusing her daughter.
He told Jamielee* that he was going to rape me and put me in hospital … she’d be watching him switch off my life support.

In another example, Tam* and his daughter Sandy* experienced online gaslighting after the disappearance of Tam’s other daughter in 2013. Gaslighting is a form of psychological manipulation that makes the victim or co-victim question their own reality.

In a bid to reinforce his alibi, the perpetrator (an acquaintance) deceived Tam and Sandy into believing they were communicating with their missing loved one. Sandy contacted the perpetrator after her sister’s disappearance, but he lied about her whereabouts and even agreed to help the family to find her.

But Sandy contacted him … on Facebook and he sent a message back, saying: ‘Oh I don’t know where she is, I had gone to bed. I was ill last night so I went to bed’ … He knew what was going to happen … he even put the rider in it to say, ‘I’ll get in touch with everybody I can to try and find out where she is’.
These examples show that the intimidation element of coercive control can be used against co-victims of intimate partner homicide in the period before their loved one is killed.

These co-victims – whether parents, siblings, friends or co-workers – fight to protect their loved one by arguing back and showing the perpetrator that his behaviour is not tolerated. However, there is a high chance that they could also put themselves in harm’s way simply by challenging the perpetrator’s behaviour and standing up for the victim.
Co-victims’ experiences should be treated as legitimate and credible in their own right. After all, they are not solely witnesses to primary victims’ experiences.

Doing so would provide a fuller understanding of coercive control, capture the wider impact of intimate partner homicide and generate more effective recommendations for prevention and support. This could improve criminal justice training on recognising and responding to the harm that co-victims experience.

articles.title: I study polling failures – this time, pollsters were mostly right, if not precise
articles.author: W Joseph Campbell, Professor Emeritus of Communication, American University School of Communication
paras: The crucial test for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate how voters are likely to decide. By that fundamental measure, the 2026 midterm polls largely succeeded in anticipating outcomes on Election Day.
If somewhat tentatively, the polls overall had been signaling important gains for Democrats. And that is what voting produced.

It was, perhaps, polling’s most reassuring performance since accurately anticipating Barack Obama’s presidential election in 2008, an outcome cited in my book, “Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in U.S. Presidential Elections.”
This is not to say the 2026 preelection polls offered precision estimates before returns poured in. They appear to have underestimated support for Democratic candidates in some Senate races.

But spot-on precision, while enviable, is not what polls can be expected to produce, considering the many ways error can infiltrate opinion surveys. Given their checkered record in recent national elections, pollsters and media analysts tended to couch their end-of-campaign assessments in measured tentativeness.

For example, Nate Cohn, chief political analyst for The New York Times, wrote just before the election that “it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. This is a real possibility. President Trump’s supporters are relatively unlikely to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.”
That risk was mostly unrealized, as Republican candidates were swept in a red wipeout.
The 2026 polls tended to confirm the truism in American politics that midterms typically are rough on candidates of the party that holds the presidency.

Another truism, again reaffirmed, is that a president’s approval ratings often are useful in gauging the country’s mood before midterm elections. President Donald Trump’s preelection approval ratings hovered at or below 40%, according to survey data compiled by RealClearPolitics.
The U.S. war with Iran, launched by Trump, was a major factor propelling the unenviable ratings. The conflict went unresolved while fuel prices surged, bringing pain to consumers.

Those and other problems prompted polling analyst Nate Silver to write that Trump “almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms. And the one superpower he has – turning out low-propensity voters in presidential years, the sorts of voters who apparently are often missed by pollsters – has never really worked when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot.”
And it didn’t work this time, either, even though throughout the campaign Trump encouraged supporters to pretend his name was on the ballot and turn out to vote.
When examined closely, the polls delivered some disagreement in the days before the election. Pollsters offered ranges that, in some races, were sizable.

For example, was Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton up by 1 percentage point in Texas late in the campaign, or was he down 7 points? Paxton lost by double digits to Democrat James Talarico, a margin that no pollster anticipated.

Similarly, was long-serving Republican Sen. Susan Collins ahead by 2 points in Maine or was she losing by 9 points? The outcome was closer to the latter reading, with Democrat Troy Jackson winning by more than six points.

In Minnesota, was Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan up by 14 points, or by just 2 points? With most votes counted by the day after the election, Flanagan’s margin of victory was about 10 points.
Such polling gaps in high-profile races offer a reminder to not focus on any single survey but, instead, to consider overall polling averages, which tend to remove or reduce the effects of outliers.

None of this necessarily is to declare that pollsters have resolved their persistent problems in sampling, especially in interviewing hard-to-reach voters. But big polling misses like that in the Texas governor’s race – where Democrat Gina Hinojosa won by double digits, although polls had shown Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ahead by a few points – were few this election cycle.
Meanwhile, the electorate’s broad inclinations were plainly if not precisely depicted.
That outcome has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-beleaguered and much-criticized cohort.

articles.title: Florida just voted for lower property taxes – and that could mean cuts in government services and new housing construction
articles.author: Abigail Hall, Professor of Economics, University of Tampa
paras: Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes.

Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis.

But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments.

While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off.
How Amendment 3 would work

Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes.

In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses.
So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters.

Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits.
But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached.

Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments.

With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups.

This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages.

State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees.

Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event.

In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties.

And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll.
A looming affordable housing crunch?

Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing.

When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall.

From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs.

Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift.
This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis.

articles.title: Pennsylvania Democrats now have power to push forward on election reform, marijuana legalization and minimum wage increases
articles.author: Daniel J. Mallinson, Associate Professor of Public Policy and Administration, Penn State
paras: The 2026 midterm elections changed the balance of power in Washington, D.C. It also proved to be a pivotal election in Pennsylvania.

Gov. Josh Shapiro handily defeated Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Not only that, it looks like Democrats will expand their majority in the state House and have flipped the state Senate, earning a 26-24 majority.
That gives Shapiro the coveted party trifecta – single party control of both the governor’s office and the General Assembly.
Given the pent-up demand among Democrats who have not fully controlled Harrisburg for over 30 years, the excitement is palpable among Pennsylvania Democrats.

I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics. Now that the political fault lines are clear for the next two years in Pennsylvania’s state government, it is worth considering what Democrats may do with their newfound power.
For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate.
Election reform has been a perennial priority in Pennsylvania since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election.

Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting where voters could vote all at once for a single party, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.

Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties in Pennsylvania to use ballot drop boxes, maintain no-excuse mail-in voting, set clear rules for ballot curing where voters are able to correct issues with their submitted mail ballots instead of having them invalidated, institute precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allow independents to vote in open primary elections.
Democrats may now be able to pass all of these without having to compromise with Republican demands for stricter voter ID requirements.

Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House passed a legalization bill in 2025. Democrats had said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they took the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization remain to be worked out, even with Democratic control.
Democrats have sponsored divergent bills on whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores, similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania.

Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the war on drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things such as expungements of past convictions, setting aside licenses for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues.

Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details. But a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania makes it even more likely that the commonwealth will be among the next states where adult-use recreational marijuana is legal.

The House has passed several measures to regulate artificial intelligence and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs, water use, local government authority and implementing and the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan.

These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda. Additionally, criticism over the AI-generated ads fielded by the Garrity campaign, which are regulated in other states, may add this issue to the state’s AI policy agenda.

Given that this election was likely heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability, Democrats will need to show progress on bringing down prices where they can. The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.

Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time. The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it also had been passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage. The legislation will have to be introduced and passed again by the new General Assembly.
Same-sex marriage and antidiscrimination

Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges decision by the U.S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent.

Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up and may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult, constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights.

Pennsylvania also does not include LGBTQ individuals in its nondiscrimination protections. The Democrats in the House passed a bill that would add sexual orientation and gender identity to the state’s Human Relations Act in 2026, but it also died in the Senate. Democrats are likely to pick this up again in 2027.
Ultimately, Democrats will not be able to do everything. They will need to decide what to prioritize and what to leave behind.

articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.author: Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California
paras: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally.

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record.
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.
Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%.
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high.
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978.

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs.
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon.
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon.

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon.

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels.

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.
As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war.

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

articles.title: ‘Epic’ blue wave helps Democrats take Congress in overwhelming rebuke to President Trump
articles.author: Charlie Hunt, Associate Professor of Political Science, Boise State University
paras: Voters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions, including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago.

Democrats took control of the House and Senate, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed.
The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections.

It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida?

There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win, and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought.

It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats.

Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district. What does that tell you?

It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties.

It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts.

I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump.

I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections.

That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending?

Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns.

This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day.

And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton. And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes.

The territory that Democrats covered is unbelievable. The South Carolina Senate race went to Annie Andrews, the Democrat, which was unfathomable even a few months ago. Mississippi still appears to be somewhat in play. The blue wave turned into something approaching a tsunami. I think a lot of Democrats saw the polling and didn’t want to believe it or couldn’t bring themselves to believe it. But some of this late polling seems to have gotten things on the mark.

What we’ve seen in these midterm elections is a massive rebuke of the last two years of the Trump administration, and a sort of blue wave of epic proportions toward the Democrats, the likes of which we haven’t seen in 20 or more years. It’s a huge confirmation of the approach that Democrats took in this election.

articles.title: Democrats in House poised to investigate the Trump Administration, taking up a long-standing power GOP-led Congress ignored for the past two years
articles.author: Drew Kurlowski, Associate Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Oversight is coming for the Trump administration.

That’s been the message of congressional Democrats throughout the closing days of the 2026 midterm campaign. Now that the party’s candidates have reportedly won control of the House of Representatives, that campaign promise is likely to be carried out. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin told The New York Times in late October that among the potential oversight targets were pardons granted by President Donald Trump, possible corruption in government contracting and the Trump family’s cryptocurrency deals.
Routine congressional oversight hearings usually don’t make headlines.
That changed during the second Trump administration.
When Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Oct. 7, 2025, what took place was a contentious, highly partisan, made-for-TV-and-social-media confrontation.
Bondi refused to answer many questions from Democrats, instead launching personal attacks against these members of the U.S. Senate.
The episode captures a basic tension in congressional oversight: Congress can demand answers, but getting them often depends on the cooperation of the branch it is investigating.
That tension is about to sharpen when Democrats control the oversight process. Their hearings will likely be anything but routine.
From our perspective as political scientists who study the U.S. Congress, congressional oversight has played an important role in American democracy. Here’s a brief history.

In simple terms, oversight is the ability of Congress to ensure that the laws it passes are faithfully executed. This generally means asking questions, demanding information, convening hearings and holding the executive branch accountable for its actions.

Oversight isn’t specifically mentioned in the Constitution. Article 1, Section 8, which lists the powers of Congress, includes the power “to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper,” without identifying an oversight role. Once laws are enacted, Article 2, Section 3, states that the president “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.”

However, the framers viewed congressional oversight as a key component of legislative authority. They wanted presidents to take Congress seriously and structured the Constitution to ensure that the executive would be accountable to the legislature.

As James Madison urged in Federalist 51, the separate branches of government should have the power to keep each other from becoming too powerful. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” Madison wrote.

The framers drew from the examples of the British Parliament and Colonial legislatures. In 1621, Sir Francis Bacon was charged with corruption and impeached as Lord High Chancellor after an investigation by a committee of the British Parliament. And in 1768, the Massachusetts Assembly conducted an investigation of Gov. Francis Bernard that led to a formal request to the King of England for his removal.

At the Federal Convention in 1787 that produced the Constitution, Delegate George Mason noted that members of Congress possessed “inquisitory powers” and “must meet frequently to inspect the Conduct of public officials.” Even though this idea was never written down, it was a habit of self-government that early Congresses put into practice.

Congressional oversight began almost as soon as the first Congress met. In 1790, Robert Morris, the superintendent of finances during the Continental Congress and a financier of the American Revolution, asked Congress to investigate his handling of the country’s finances and was exonerated of any wrongdoing.

During this period, congressional investigations were often referred to select committees – bodies created to perform special functions. These panels had the power to issue subpoenas and hold individuals in contempt. Since there was no official record of debates and proceedings, the public relied on newspaper accounts to learn about what had happened.

In March 1792, congressional oversight exposed businessman William Duer, who signed contracts with the War Department but failed to furnish the needed military supplies. This shortfall contributed to a stunning U.S. military defeat against a confederation of Native American tribes in the Northwest Territory.
Congress eventually removed the quartermaster general from his role for mismanaging the contracts.
Throughout the 19th century, Congress continued to quietly exercise this power.

Hearings from December 1861 to May 1865 on the conduct of the U.S. Civil War produced a detailed record of the war, exposed military wrongdoing and condemned slavery. In 1871, the Senate created a select committee to investigate Ku Klux Klan violence during Reconstruction.
Investigating corruption and criminal acts
Congress started to use its oversight power more aggressively in the 1920s with the Senate Committee on Public Land and Surveys’ high-profile investigations into the Teapot Dome scandal.

Hearings revealed that Interior Secretary Albert Bacon Fall had secretly leased federal oil reserves in Wyoming to two private corporations and had received personal loans and gifts from the companies in return.
The investigation found clear evidence of corruption. Fall was indicted and became the first U.S. Cabinet member to be convicted of a felony.

The U.S. Supreme Court helped to shape the legal foundation of congressional oversight. In McGrain v. Daugherty, decided in 1927, the court held that congressional committees could issue subpoenas, force witnesses to testify and hold them in contempt if they fail to appear. Two years later, in Sinclair v. United States, the court ruled that witnesses who lied to Congress could be charged with perjury.
These cases granted the judicial branch’s sanction to what had long been an implied legislative power, cementing the constitutionality of congressional oversight.
The modern era of congressional oversight has produced some very important reforms – and some truly regrettable spectacles.

The most important example of bipartisan congressional oversight came in response to reporting by The Washington Post’s Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward. The two journalists wrote about the 1972 burgling of Democratic National Committee offices in Washington, D.C.’s Watergate Hotel and subsequent cover-up efforts by the Nixon administration – and President Richard Nixon himself.

On Feb. 7, 1973, the U.S. Senate voted 77-0 to establish a Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, which brought together Democrats and Republicans to investigate what came to be known as the “Watergate scandal.” The committee’s work spurred action in Congress to impeach Nixon, leading to Nixon’s resignation in 1974 and to the enactment of legal reforms to provide an institutional check on presidential power.

Another high point for congressional oversight came after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001. Seeking to learn how the deadliest terrorist strike on American soil had occurred, Democratic Sen. Bob Graham and Republican Rep. Porter Goss, who chaired the Senate and House Intelligence committees, formed a joint committee to investigate intelligence failures before and after the attacks.

This inquiry produced several important recommendations that were ultimately adopted, including the creation of a director of national intelligence and a Department of Homeland Security, as well as better information sharing among law enforcement agencies.

Congress’ oversight can extend beyond the executive branch when the actions of private actors raise questions about existing laws or spur the need for new ones. Investigations into medical device safety and Enron’s 2001 collapse examined malfeasance in the private sphere that existing regulations failed to prevent.

However, the power to expose corruption can also be used as a tool to score partisan points and generate outrage, rather than holding the executive branch accountable for actual malfeasance. Notably, in the 1950s, Wisconsin Sen. Joseph McCarthy turned oversight into inquisition and used the power of media to amplify his accusations of communist influence within the federal government.

As we see it, the problem with allowing oversight to become political theater is that it distracts Congress from quieter and more meaningful oversight work. Slow, procedural work isn’t likely to go viral, but it helps keep government accountable. The task of a deliberate legislative body is to reconcile those very different impulses.
Congressional oversight has strengthened the democratic system at many points. But it can also be stymied by an uncooperative executive branch.

After the 2018 midterm elections put Democrats in charge of the House of Representatives, their many attempts to exercise oversight were rejected by the first Trump administration, which refused to send officials to testify at hearings, failed to turn over documents and ignored subpoenas.
Will the next two years of divided government look the same?
